title: Analysis: How the UK spent more than £11.6bn on climate aid since 2021 - Carbon Brief
gist: FOI data show the UK provided £12.8bn of climate finance in 2021-22 to 2025-26 (record £4bn in 2025-26), beating its £11.6bn target only via £2.2bn of reclassified existing aid; the next three-year pledge of around £6bn implies roughly £2bn a year, about half the current level.

insights.claim: The UK provided £12.8bn of climate finance to developing countries between 2021-22 and 2025-26, exceeding its £11.6bn target, according to FOI data obtained by Carbon Brief.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Establishes the actual size of UK public climate flows, a baseline for climate-finance and development-bank exposure.

insights.claim: UK climate finance reached a record £4bn in 2025-26, roughly a tenfold nominal increase from 2011-12 when the UK began providing it.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Peak year; the next phase starts from a much lower run-rate, so flows to recipient funds fall.
insights.locator: UK climate aid has reached record levels

insights.claim: At least 493 projects, funds and institutions received UK climate finance over the five years, including £45m for Ukraine to curb fossil-fuel reliance, £40m of drought cash transfers in Kenya and £30m for flood resilience in Nepal.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Shows how fragmented and humanitarian-leaning the book of projects is.
insights.locator: The UK has supported around 500 climate projects since 2021

insights.claim: The UK does not routinely publish climate-finance data broken down by financial year, making progress towards its target impossible to gauge accurately; UN reporting comes with a two-year lag.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Opacity means FOI-derived trackers are the main reliable data source for monitoring donor commitments.
insights.locator: The UK has supported around 500 climate projects since 2021

insights.claim: The £11.6bn target was met only because the government reclassified £2.2bn of existing foreign aid as climate finance without spending any more.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Headline target attainment overstates new money delivered; discount donor climate-finance claims accordingly.

insights.claim: In March 2026 the Labour government committed to about £6bn of UK aid as climate finance over three years instead of a new five-year goal, averaging roughly £2bn a year, about half the 2025-26 level.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Expect a step-down in UK-funded climate flows from 2026-27, lowering demand-side support for funds and MDB climate lines.
insights.locator: Rather than setting a new five-year goal

insights.claim: The £6bn three-year pledge is a significant real-terms reduction from the £11.6bn pledge once accounting changes and inflation are factored in.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Headline numbers hide a larger cut in real, additional money.
insights.locator: This amounts to a significant reduction

insights.claim: Alongside the £6bn of aid, the UK pledged £6.7bn from outside the aid budget in private investments, export credit and guarantees to development banks, forms of support the UK already provided but had not counted towards climate-finance targets.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Shifts UK climate finance toward guarantees and export credit, favouring private capital mobilisation over grants.

insights.claim: The UK, like other major donors such as the US, has dramatically cut its aid budget, placing significant strain on its climate finance.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Aid-budget cuts across donors are a headwind for adaptation and climate-fund flows.
insights.locator: alongside other major donors, such as the US

insights.claim: More than 80% of UK climate finance since 2021 was delivered multilaterally and is listed as supporting 'developing countries' generally or whole regions; only £2.1bn (17%) was bilateral.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Most UK money flows through funds and institutions, so their governance and absorption capacity matter more than country projects.
insights.locator: The vast majority of UK climate finance was delivered

insights.claim: Afghanistan overtook Ethiopia as the top bilateral recipient with £256m labelled climate-related versus £226m, because the UK automatically labels 30% of humanitarian aid to the country as climate finance rather than due to new climate initiatives.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Rankings of climate-finance recipients reflect accounting rules as much as climate need.

insights.claim: The same 30% humanitarian-aid labelling made war-torn Somalia (£139m), Sudan (£136m) and Yemen (£130m) top recipients of UK climate aid.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Shows how reclassification inflates climate-labelled flows to conflict states.
insights.locator: This shift affected other climate-vulnerable and war-torn nations

insights.claim: Large UK climate sums to middle-income countries are mainly aimed at mobilising private investment, such as £83m to Brazil's Amazon Fund and £43m to boost UK investment in India's low-carbon infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Public money is being used as catalytic capital for carbon-offset and low-carbon infrastructure plays.
insights.locator: Where the UK has provided large sums

insights.claim: The UK channelled £198m into a World Bank-backed project helping Colombia, Cambodia and others create and sell 'high-integrity' carbon offsets, and £229m to a group using aid to attract private capital for projects such as a Ugandan solar farm and a Pakistani sustainable aviation fuel project.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Public funds are seeding carbon-credit supply and blended-finance pipelines in emerging markets.
insights.locator: Larger sums were provided to projects spread across multiple countries

themes.theme: Development banks and BII as delivery channels

insights.claim: The Green Climate Fund received £1.5bn from the UK, more than any other initiative, despite the UK recently cutting its 2024-27 support for the fund.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: The UN's flagship fund remains the largest single UK recipient even as its funding is trimmed.

insights.claim: British International Investment, a publicly owned for-profit company partly supported by UK aid, received almost £1.4bn of UK climate finance, and the UK is increasingly relying on it to meet climate-finance goals as it prioritises clean-energy over fossil fuels.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: BII is a growing conduit for UK-backed clean-energy investment in developing markets.

insights.claim: Multilateral development banks, particularly World Bank arms and the African Development Bank, are major recipients because the UK started counting core funding for these banks as climate finance.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: MDB core contributions now count toward climate goals, reinforcing their role as the main channel.
insights.locator: Other major recipients of UK climate finance

insights.claim: The UK's accounting changes, which boosted BII and multilateral banks, have been criticised by experts, MPs and the UK's aid watchdog.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Political and oversight risk to how the UK counts climate finance.
